1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient is a 65-year-old woman. Chief complaint: "Dyspnea for 13 years with worsening for 1 month, with acute onset on the last day." Thirteen years before admission, she had persistent unexplained episodes of sudden dyspnea and chest tightness, and was diagnosed with "left pneumothorax, pulmonary bullae." She improved and was discharged after closed thoracic drainage. After discharge, her condition gradually manifested as "palpitations and dyspnea after activity, cough and sputum production without obvious triggers." Two years ago, she was diagnosed at another hospital with "COPD, pulmonary bullae" and was treated with regular inhalation of "Symbicort." She reported poor efficacy and discontinued the medication on her own. One month ago, she developed a sudden "right pneumothorax" and underwent right closed thoracic drainage at another hospital, with relief, but her dyspnea improved only minimally. One day before admission, upon getting up in the morning, she again developed dyspnea and worsening chest tightness. In the emergency department, she was diagnosed with "right pneumothorax, pulmonary bullae" and was admitted to the department after right closed thoracic drainage. Recently, her mental status, sleep, and appetite have been fair; she feels easy fatigability and shortness of breath with minimal activity. Bowel and bladder habits are normal. Three months ago, she was diagnosed at West China Second University Hospital with "endometrial thickening"; biopsy showed HPV+, and she received vaginal packing treatment with "recombinant interferon." One month ago, she underwent "endoscopic gastric polypectomy" at another hospital. More than 20 years ago, she received 1 blood transfusion during childbirth. She denies smoking, alcohol use, and drug abuse. Her father had "lung disease" and died of "rectal cancer" 1 year ago; her sister and younger brother both have "pulmonary bullae." Physical examination: temperature 36.8℃, heart rate 108 beats/min, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, blood pressure 162/99mmHg. She was alert, appeared acutely ill, had a barrel chest, increased bilateral chest wall respiratory excursion, and a closed drainage tube connected to the right chest wall. Percussion of both lungs was hyperresonant, and a few moist rales were heard at the bases of both lungs; the cardiac silhouette was slightly enlarged, heart rhythm was regular, and no obvious murmurs were heard in any valve area; the abdomen was normal in contour, soft throughout, without tenderness or rebound tenderness, no abdominal mass was palpable, the liver and spleen were not palpable below the costal margins, and both kidneys were not palpable. There was no edema of either lower extremity.

differential_diagnoses.name: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (predominantly right-sided, with a history of recurrent bilateral episodes)
supporting_evidence: Chief complaint: dyspnea for 13 years with worsening for 1 month, with acute onset on the last day
13 years ago, was diagnosed with left-sided pneumothorax and pulmonary bullae; improved after closed thoracic drainage.
Sudden onset of "right-sided pneumothorax" 1 month ago, relieved after right closed thoracic drainage at an outside hospital
1 day before admission, dyspnea recurred with worsening chest tightness; in the emergency department, he was diagnosed with "right pneumothorax, pulmonary bulla"
Physical examination showed "a closed thoracic drainage tube connected to the right chest wall"
Physical examination showed respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, heart rate 108 beats/min, and an acutely ill appearance.
Hyperresonance to percussion over both lungs, suggesting increased intrathoracic air content or pulmonary hyperinflation
opposing_evidence: The phase 1 information did not provide clear contradictory evidence.

differential_diagnoses.name: Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome (familial pulmonary cyst/pulmonary bulla-related disease)
supporting_evidence: The patient is female, denies smoking, yet has a long history of recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax and "pulmonary bullae".
Left-sided pneumothorax 13 years ago; right-sided pneumothorax 1 month ago and on this occasion, indicating recurrent bilateral episodes
Both his older sister and younger brother have bullae of the lung, and his father has lung disease, suggesting a clear familial clustering.
Long-term palpitations and dyspnea after exertion, consistent with one of the chronic manifestations of diffuse cystic lung disease
Previous inhaled treatment for "COPD and bullous emphysema" was ineffective, suggesting it may not be simple, common COPD.
opposing_evidence: Phase 1 did not mention accompanying clues such as fibrofolliculomas of the skin, renal tumors, or renal cysts.
In phase 1, no description of the distribution characteristics of pulmonary cysts on chest imaging was provided.

differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease/emphysema with pulmonary bullae
supporting_evidence: Previously diagnosed at another hospital with "COPD, pulmonary bullae"
Long-standing "palpitations and dyspnea on exertion," and "fatigue and shortness of breath with minimal activity"
Physical examination showed barrel chest and hyperresonance to percussion of both lungs, consistent with signs of pulmonary hyperinflation.
Recurrent pneumothorax may be caused by rupture of pulmonary bullae
A small amount of moist rales is heard in the lower portions of both lungs, which may be seen in chronic airway/pulmonary parenchymal lesions with superimposed infection or retained secretions.
opposing_evidence: Denies smoking, reducing support for the common smoking-related COPD
Regular use of Symbicort by inhalation; the patient reports poor efficacy
There is obvious familial clustering of "pulmonary bullae/lung disease," suggesting possible hereditary or other specific cystic lung disease rather than typical COPD.

differential_diagnoses.name: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)
supporting_evidence: Female patient with long-term progressive dyspnea and recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax
Previously informed multiple times of "pulmonary bullae," and dyspnea did not completely improve after closed thoracic drainage, suggesting possible diffuse structural lung abnormality.
Denies smoking, which helps distinguish it from some smoking-related cystic lung diseases
opposing_evidence: Age 65 years, older than the age at onset commonly seen in LAM
There is a clear family clustering of “pulmonary bullae/lung disease,” while the typical familial clustering of LAM is not prominent.
Phase 1 did not mention chylothorax, renal angiomyolipoma, or manifestations related to tuberous sclerosis.

differential_diagnoses.name: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency-related emphysema/bullous lung disease
supporting_evidence: Denies smoking, yet has long-standing progressive dyspnea, barrel chest, hyperresonance, and "pulmonary bullae"
Recurrent bilateral pneumothorax can occur in the setting of severe bullous emphysema.
The father and siblings have "lung disease/pulmonary bullae," suggesting possible genetic susceptibility.
opposing_evidence: No related clues such as liver disease or jaundice were mentioned in the first stage.
Phase 1 did not provide imaging information such as the distribution characteristics of emphysema.
At age 65, first recognized by the system is atypical, but a milder form or late-onset presentation cannot be excluded.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis or other diffuse cystic lung disease
supporting_evidence: Recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax and manifestations of bullae/cystic destructive lung disease
Long-term progressive dyspnea, with poor response to routine treatment for "COPD," suggesting that rare cystic lung disease should be considered
opposing_evidence: Denies smoking, not supportive of typical pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis
Familial clustering is more suggestive of hereditary cystic lung disease than this disease
No clues such as nodules, upper-lung-predominant involvement, or extrapulmonary involvement were provided in the first stage.

stage2_input.text: Laboratory tests: [CBC] NEUT% 77.2%; [DIC panel] normal; [Biochemistry] liver and renal function and electrolytes normal; [Pre-transfusion panel] hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, syphilis (-); [Thyroid function] normal; [Urinalysis and stool routine] normal; [Serum tumor markers] normal; [Blood gas analysis] pH 7.408, PCO2 39.3 mmHg, PO2 154.5 mmHg, BE -0.3 mmol/L, HCO3- 24.2 mmol/L, SPO2 99.6%, FiO2 21%. Infection-related markers: ESR 33 mm/h, CRP 3.82 mg/L, IL6 4.92 pg/ml, PCT <0.02 ng/ml; T-SPOT (-); G test (-), GM test (-); sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli and sputum bacterial/fungal cultures were all negative. Immune-related markers: ANA, ENA (-); ANCA (-); anticardiolipin antibody (-); alpha-1 antitrypsin (-). Echocardiography: no obvious abnormalities in cardiac structure or blood flow; measured left ventricular systolic function was normal. Chest CT: Day 0: right hydropneumothorax, drainage tube shadow seen, approximately 40% compression of the lung, partial atelectatic consolidation of the right lung; emphysema, multiple bullae in both lungs, scattered inflammation in both lungs. No cardiac enlargement; small pericardial effusion. Day +11: small right hydropneumothorax, drainage tube shadow seen, small amount of gas in the right chest wall and root of the neck; emphysema, multiple bullae in both lungs, scattered inflammation in both lungs. Mixed ground-glass nodule in the right lower lobe, approximately 0.4 cm in diameter. No cardiac enlargement; small pericardial effusion. Abdominal CT: no obvious abnormality.

differential_diagnoses.name: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)
evidence: The patient is a woman and does not smoke.
Symptoms manifested as recurrent dyspnea and spontaneous pneumothorax
Imaging showed diffusely distributed low-density air-filled cystic lesions in both lungs, with the lung parenchyma between the cystic spaces being approximately normal.
exclusion_reasons: Imaging suggests bilateral pulmonary cystic lesions of varying sizes, with a large area of cystic lesions; the largest has a diameter greater than 10 mm, which is not consistent with the diffuse bilateral small cystic airspace opacities seen in LAM.
Clinical manifestations do not include any of the following: tuberous sclerosis complex, renal angiomyolipoma, lymphangioleiomyoma, chylothorax, or chylous ascites

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (PLCH)
evidence: The patient's imaging showed multiple bilateral pulmonary cysts of varying sizes and diverse morphology.
exclusion_reasons: The patient is a middle-aged to older adult woman and does not smoke.
Imaging shows diffuse bilateral pulmonary cysts, not predominantly in the upper and middle lungs, and no multiple small nodules in both lungs

recommended_exams.exam: Peripheral blood sent for whole-exome sequencing
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Arrange for the patient to undergo whole-exome sequencing on peripheral blood.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a 65-year-old woman with recurrent bilateral spontaneous pneumothoraces and progressive dyspnea over the past 13 years. In the past month, a right-sided pneumothorax recurred, and dyspnea improved only minimally after closed thoracic drainage. Repeated chest CT showed multiple pulmonary bullae/thin-walled cystic lesions in both lungs with emphysema, while the patient denied smoking; previous inhaled treatment for COPD had poor efficacy, suggesting that this is not typical smoking-related COPD. At the same time, her father had “lung disease,” and both her sister and younger brother had “pulmonary bullae,” indicating clear familial aggregation, which makes hereditary diffuse cystic lung disease, especially Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, a key diagnostic consideration. Earlier evaluations, including imaging, immunologic, infectious, and α1-antitrypsin testing, had largely excluded LAM, PLCH, LIP, infectious causes, and some immune-related causes, but molecular genetic evidence for a definitive diagnosis is still lacking. Whole-exome sequencing was arranged on peripheral blood, mainly to look for pathogenic mutations in FLCN and other genes, in order to fundamentally confirm whether this is BHD or another hereditary cystic lung disease; this would not only help establish a definitive diagnosis and exclude other nonhereditary differential diagnoses, but also directly affect subsequent explanation of the risk of recurrent pneumothorax, screening of family members and genetic counseling, and the further development of a multisystem follow-up plan targeting BHD-related pulmonary, renal, and other manifestations.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Arrange peripheral blood for whole-exome sequencing. The results indicated the presence of an FLCN gene mutation.

diagnostic_basis: Basic characteristics: middle-aged or older woman; her father had "lung disease" (specific details unclear); her older sister and younger brother both have pulmonary bullae.
Symptoms: recurrent dyspnea for 13 years, recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax.

Physical signs: barrel chest; increased bilateral thoracic respiratory excursion; a closed chest drainage tube connected to the right chest wall; hyperresonance to percussion over both lungs; a few moist rales heard at the lower portions of both lungs.

Additional examinations: Chest CT: right hydropneumothorax, with a tube shadow visible; approximately 40% compression of the lung parenchyma; partial atelectatic consolidation of the right lung; emphysema; multiple bullae in both lungs; scattered inflammation in both lungs. ESR 33 mm/h, slightly elevated; arterial blood gas analysis showed no hypoxemia. Whole-exome sequencing indicated the presence of an FLCN gene mutation.
Meets 1 major criterion (presence of an FLCN gene mutation)

treatment_plan: After admission, continuous closed thoracic drainage was administered.
treatment_response: After discharge, the patient developed one episode of pneumothorax and underwent closed thoracic drainage again.
